k-1.x_notes: Strengths: header, footer and the one-time shared rule match the organizer's format, with no Name field. All boards are printed at actual size. Five block-based problems, each with several items: P1 asks for every way to fill the hexagon with green, blue and red (7 combinations, 9 outlines, children color each way). P2 asks for the fewest blocks on three shapes, and the size-3 triangle has a non-greedy answer of 3 trapezoids. P3 asks whether blue alone can cover five shapes (yes/no/yes/no/yes); two of the 'no' shapes have an even number of triangles but more up than down. P4 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (answers 2, 3, 4). P5 asks for every blue tiling of the hexagons (2 tilings for one size, 3 for the other), which is an entry point to kernel 2. All answers check out. Weaknesses: P3 only asks children to circle yes or no and never asks why. Children color answers rather than invent anything. Five problems will fill the time, but with little to spare.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: seven problems with real reasoning, all at actual size. P1 asks which single colors can fill the hexagon, and purple is a good 'no' case. P2 finds the 10 combinations (12 outlines). P3 counts triangles (4, 9, 16) and predicts 25 for side 5. P4 asks for the fewest greens and predicts 5 for side 5. P5 asks which six shapes blue can fill (no/yes/yes/no/yes/no, including an even-area impossible shape) and asks 'how do you know?'. P6 asks for the fewest pieces. P7 asks children to invent 6- and 8-triangle shapes that blue cannot fill, which is an excellent open task. All answers check out. Weaknesses: there is a Name field on every page, the header has no week or activity, and the footer is only a page number. P1 is short. P3 leans toward counting practice. Children have to draw their answers rather than color them, and there is no rhombus-tiling task leading toward kernel 2.
k-1.reason: Both are concrete and correct. Y gives K–1 more substantial work, a 'how do you know' prompt and an invent-a-shape problem, so it does not end early. X's pages are cleaner and include a nice rhombus-tiling task, but its problems are more closed.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: clean format, actual-size boards, and recording space plus writing lines throughout. The problems develop kernel 1 in a clear order. P1 has four boards, two impossible because of extra up triangles. P2 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 2 to 5. P3 asks whether chevrons can ever help (they cannot, because each chevron splits into two blues). P4 shows four copies of the same hexagon with two black triangles each; I checked them: J and M are impossible (two triangles of the same color removed) and K and L can be covered. P5 asks for the proof, then side 10. P6 asks for a 16-triangle board that needs as many greens as possible; the true maximum is 6, which makes a good open extremal problem. Weaknesses: P5 prints 'at least 4', which gives away the bound. P1 never asks why. Every impossible board fails only because of the up/down imbalance.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: a richer and more varied set of contrasting boards. P1 includes an odd-area board, two boards with more of one color than the other, and an irregular board with equal counts that can be covered. P4's board J has 7 up and 7 down triangles yet cannot be covered, because two down triangles both depend on the same single up triangle; this shows that equal counts are not enough. P2 has board F (holes of opposite colors, can be covered) and board G (two down holes, cannot). P3 asks for which pairs of holes the rest of the hexagon can be covered. I checked all 144 pairs by computer, and the answer is cleanly 'exactly when one hole points up and one points down', which makes this a lovely open problem in the spirit of the mutilated chessboard. P5 asks for the fewest greens on triangles of side 3 to 6 at actual size. P6 asks for side 10 and side 100 with the reason. P7 and P8 ask good two-way questions about chevrons. Weaknesses: there is a Name field and a nonstandard header and footer. There is no space to record answers or explanations for P1–P4 or P6–P7, and P6–P8 are crowded onto one page.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are mathematically sound and will keep third graders busy. Y's balanced-but-impossible board and its open question about where two holes can go add real depth beyond the colour count. X's pages are tidier and include recording space, and Y's page problems can be fixed quickly.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: clean format, actual-size boards, plenty of small copies for drawing, and writing lines. The problems build one complete argument. P1 asks for the tilings of the n,1,1 hexagons (2, 3, 4, so 11 for top edge 10). P2 asks for the 6 tilings of the 2,2,1 hexagon. P3 asks for the fewest flips between pictured tilings: I checked that S and T are the two extreme tilings (8 flips), S to U is 3, and U to T is 5. P4 defines the chains with a correct worked example and gives four letter pairs; I checked that two pairs are possible and two are not, and U reappears as one of the pairs. P5 counts the 20 tilings (25 copies, so the number is not given away). P6 asks what a flip does to the letters (it swaps one adjacent pair). P7 asks for the lower bound and the parity argument. Weaknesses: P6 breaks the discovery into directed recording steps. P7 states 'at least 8'. The chain definition is long. Children never draw the whole flip graph, and stacks of cubes never appear.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: concise, open questions that cover the outline broadly. P1 asks for the 6 coverings of the 1,2,2 hexagon. P2 has children draw the whole flip graph and find the two coverings farthest apart (4 flips). P3 introduces ribbons with a correct example and asks whether a ribbon determines its covering (it does). P4 asks for board B (10 coverings) and the 1,4,4 hexagon (70), a real ribbon-to-counting generalization. P5 asks for the 20 coverings of the size-2 hexagon. P6: I checked that its two pictured coverings are valid and the answer is 4 flips. P7 asks which coverings are farthest apart (8 flips). P8 asks whether a round trip can take an odd number of flips. P9 connects tilings to stacks of cubes. Weaknesses: there is a Name field and a nonstandard header and footer. P4 and P6–P9 have no answer space. Ribbons are developed only for boards with a single ribbon, so counting the size-2 hexagon and the parity question lack the bridge that 'a flip swaps an adjacent L and R' would give. Some layout is awkward: board B sits a page after its question.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are excellent and correct. X builds the full kernel-2 argument (chains count the tilings, a flip swaps a letter pair, so round trips are even and S to T needs 8) with workspace for it. Y adds the flip graph and the cubes but leaves the step from ribbons to flips to the adult.

overall.reason: Neither packet has a broken problem, and both put concrete block work first. Y gives K–1 more and deeper work and gives grades 2–3 sharper contrasting boards, including a board that is impossible despite equal counts and the open question about where two holes can go. X is slightly better for grades 4–5 and follows the page format far more closely. Y's flaws (the Name field, header and footer, and missing answer space) can be fixed within the editing time, while X's thinner spots would need new problems.
